: Thank you, Madam Speaker.
NANCY LU (National): As I stand to commend the Appropriation (2026/27 Estimates) Bill third reading to the House, I want to first acknowledge Paul, who came all the way from Christchurch, who’s with us in the gallery today. Welcome to Wellington. Welcome to your House. I hope you feel very special that you’re welcomed by members across the party, because we are elected by people like Paul to be in the House to fight for things that will build a better future for New Zealand. It’s very welcoming to actually see how people like Paul engage with how we pass bills to make it better for New Zealand.
: At heart, this bill is about choices. It is about how, as a National-led Government, we use taxpayers’ money more responsibly, where we choose to invest to return the biggest impact that we can for the public sector and for New Zealanders, and what kind of New Zealand we want in the future and the economy that we want to build, to leave a lasting legacy for the future generations of New Zealand. There was so much that this Government needed to fix when we inherited it from the last lot, but our priorities are very clear: it is about fixing the basics and building a better future for all New Zealanders. I’ve had so many notes to write about—one part on fixing the basics, one part on building the future; what we have done in the last three; what this Budget is adding to what we’ve done in the last three years, but also, the bill as it laps over the next four years and what we are building for New Zealand.
: In terms of fixing the basics, I have to start with health. Health is often, especially now, at the end of winter time, what people talk about when I door-knock on the weekend and what people tell me about on the doorstep. When I’ve shared with them that the current Government has invested, in our Budget, a record $5.5 billion extra—extra—of taxpayers’ money into front-line health services over the forecast, they’ve been quite surprised. Then they’ve asked me questions and we’ve gone deeper into the bureaucracies that we inherited from the last lot; what happens in healthcare. However, we’ve told them the plan and what we’re doing already, including the additional spending that we put in into this year’s Budget, including new hospitals and new wards built around the country—that is the new hospital wing in Dunedin, that is the new hospital we’re now building for Whangārei, that is the new land we’re purchasing for South Auckland, that is also feeding and building into the future of front-line doctors and nurses by doing the additional school in Waikato University.
: Apart from the hospital, the wards, the beds, it is also the additional money we’ve put into Pharmac medicine. It is also about putting in funding and support for more precautionary and prevention testing—into breast cancer screening, into cervical screening, into bowel cancer screening. All of this is adding and helping towards building a better future for New Zealanders.
: Then, what are we fixing in education? I am a mother of two young children, and when I sent Amber to her first day in school, I sent a text message to the Minister of Education, Minister Erica Stanford. I thanked her as a voter in New Zealand, and I thanked her as a mother, because myself, having gone through the public school system, I had all the confidence in the New Zealand public school system until the last lot came in, when there was rising truancy and kids were not going to school any more. There was no clear understanding from schools, from teachers, and from parents on what to teach our children. There was no foundational skills or knowledge taught in maths and English, and definitely not in science.
: So what are we fixing? We are fixing it. I literally just saw this and I thought it was so fitting—I hope the TV will see it, and people around New Zealand will see it. While Labour are talking “tax, tax, tax”, we are building, and this is without adding additional tax on New Zealand taxpayers. We as a Government are building 1,364 new classrooms—1,364 new classrooms—without adding new taxes. We’ve built three new specialist schools without adding new taxes. We are also adding solar panels to 500 schools around the country to help to reduce their energy bills, to help to provide a safer and warmer school for our children, without adding new taxes. That is what I call fixing the basics but also building the future—this is what the National Government is about.
: Then there’s law and order. I remember door-knocking in 2023 and that was the number one thing talked about in our community. There was concern about going into shopping malls, concern about ram raids, and concern about all the young children getting out of school or not going to school and then creating chaos and mayhem. There was concern about gangs going into townships and closing down townships so kids can’t go to school. There was a lot of anxiety and fear in the community.
: So we came in, and what did we do in fixing the basics—and what has this Budget added? Just look at the results now. Ram raids are down by 85 percent, there are new police stations because the Government invested in a new police station in Greymouth, a new police station in Whanganui, and for Corrections a new courthouse in Rotorua. All of that was added, and the result we’re seeing now is a 22 percent reduction in serious repeat youth offending and 46,000 fewer victims—victims and their families—and better, safer communities.
: That sort of fixing the basics needs to continue. We still have too much crime, but we cannot afford to go back to the last lot, which has, by the way, the same leader, the same deputy leader, the same front bench—just swapped around because they don’t answer emails—and all the same team, and they’re going back to the same strategy of all talk and no delivery. Actually, there is additional talk, because they’ve now promised tax, tax, tax, and also because their potential coalition partners are now talking about a bottom line being adding taxes, taxes, taxes. What do they have to show for it? Nothing.
: In the last week when I door-knocked, people were concerned about the additional tax burden. Fundamentally, they are saying, “We don’t mind so much about paying tax, but we know that we’re just giving our money for no reason. We know that we’re just giving all this money to the IRD and we don’t see new hospitals, new roads, new schools—nothing.”
: I want to answer one of the comments made by a speaker in the Labour Party just before me. He talked about the growing number of businesses closing down. He probably hasn’t read the news, because actually at the year ended 31 July 2026 there were more companies registered at the Companies Office—far more; actually, 40 percent more new businesses registered than businesses closed. If you are going to read one side of the stats, just make sure that you read the other side so that you have the complete, accurate story, because whatever we say in this House has a growing impact outside this House. People listen, so give them the true story.
: Anyway, what are we doing for the future? This Government, in this Budget, has committed to infrastructure pipeline projects—and we have started turning the sod—that in the next four years will bring 220,000 new jobs for New Zealand. Those jobs will come with construction, with all the different sectors that are related to the projects, like new roads, new bridges, but also in retail and all the hospitality and service providers that come around those infrastructure projects. Remember that when we talk about the new infrastructure we’re putting in.
: Also, there are record-breaking export sales. We are a migrant country. We are also a country that focuses so much on exports. We do so well at producing primary goods, so let’s not forget about the policies we have implemented and are supporting through Investment Boost and through a boost to families.
: Also, KiwiSaver can now be used for first-home buyers on farms. All those measures are to help our primary sector to make sure that they continue to deliver and to grow this economy. This is why I think people at this year’s election have a very, very clear choice. It is about a party vote for parties that are mature, that have a plan, and are already delivering on the plan, and we have shown in the records that we have actually fixed the basics, but we are also building the future at the same time.
: This election, make sure that you vote. Make sure that you vote for the party that will actually drive delivery, growth, and provide better jobs and a better future for all New Zealanders. I commend the bill to the House.
Hon KIERAN McANULTY (Labour): Thank you, Madam Speaker. That was quite an extraordinary contribution. Government members are trying to have New Zealanders believe that they have somehow managed to lower taxes, increase spending, and reduce debt. Oh, no, they didn’t mention debt, did they? No, and there’s a very good reason for that. They have tried to present this to New Zealanders—that somehow they have managed to do all these things without raising taxes. That is what they are trying to push.
: But, as Nancy Lu was pleading with the House to tell the whole story, let’s have the whole story. This Government has borrowed through the teeth to get the things that are in this Budget. They have not balanced the books like they promised. In fact, they have increased the debt. This Government have borrowed more than the previous Government did, if you exclude COVID. Let’s now include COVID, because during that time the very same MPs that are now senior Ministers were pleading with us to spend more. They cannot have it both ways.
: They are trying to trick New Zealanders into believing that it is possible to do all these things that they have promised without increasing taxes and without increasing debt. It is not possible. It is not true. That is why they are not telling the full story. The thing is that a few speeches—even speeches read today on that side of the House—are not going to change the reality for New Zealanders. They know that what Nancy Lu just said isn’t true. They know that what Mike Butterick said before her isn’t true. It doesn’t add up.
Rima Nakhle: Best MP.
Hon KIERAN McANULTY: I’m not at all surprised to hear that Rima Nakhle’s piping up. She may as well make the most of the time she’s got. My pick, with two parliamentary sitting weeks left and just over two months left before the election, is that she’s gone, and so is Tim Costley as well.
: New Zealanders know that this Government promised the world and has delivered nothing. Things have got worse. Debt has increased. Costs have increased. Wages have gone down in real terms. Unemployment is up. Homelessness is up. None of those things was talked about in any of the contributions from the Government members today.
: What is also fascinating is that none of them has talked about nurses. Why is that, I wonder. Why is that? Is it possibly because the Prime Minister and the health Minister—and basically all of them—have been caught out? They have been caught out misleading the country by saying they have added 2,000 more nurses, but, actually, that is not true, is it? No, it’s not true. The number is 54—54 nurses at a time when demand on the health system has never been higher. This lot have only increased the number of nurses by 54.
: Why is it, I wonder, that they have to make things up. Why do they have to claim that it’s 2,000 when it is actually 54? It is not just in terms of nurses, by the way. They are claiming that they have built 7,000 houses when, actually, it’s 600. Why do they have to make things up? It’s because their record doesn’t stand on its own two feet. It falls over very quickly once you scratch the surface, once you get through the spin, once you get through all the nonsense, all the PR—it doesn’t stack up.
: Just look at the record in nursing. Waikato Hospital has 90 fewer fulltime-equivalents than a year ago. That’s extraordinary. Auckland City Hospital has 74 fewer. Middlemore Hospital has 78 fewer. They have not added a single nurse to Wairarapa Hospital in their entire time in Government. In fact, Wairarapa are 40 nurses short, and they are not allowed to hire. Let that sink in: they are 40 nurses short of what we need, and they are not allowed to hire, because Simeon Brown and this Government have put a hiring freeze on. They are not allowed to hire.
: Is it any wonder that the number of nurses has grown by only 54 in this term? It is outrageous, and the fact that they tried to fib, the fact that they tried to mislead the country into thinking it was more when it was only 54, says everything you need to know about this Government. Just look at Palmerston North. They’ve had 25 cut in the last two years. Northland has had 67 cut, and Nelson-Marlborough has been cut by 30. They are going backwards because they have not invested in health. When they say they’ve done all these things, put a record level of funding into health, you only need to increase it by a dollar for it to be a record level of funding.
: The thing is that they have not kept up with demand; they have not kept up with the cost.
Rima Nakhle: In six years, they couldn’t even bring in free breast cancer screening.
Hon KIERAN McANULTY: They are chirping away because I have hit a nerve—because they’re going around their communities knocking on doors and telling people that nurses have gone up by 2,000 when they know it isn’t true. Why are they saying things they know are not true? It’s because they know that if they actually talked the truth when it came to nurses, it would not stack up.
: It is exactly the same when you look at the claims that were made around Wairarapa Hospital. This is an issue that I have been banging on about for the last three years. This Government stole money that was intended to fix our hospital. We had to get the Speaker involved because the Minister refused to answer questions. We had to get the Ombudsman involved because the health ministry refused to answer questions. There was money designated to fix Wairarapa Hospital, they took it to fix the hole in their Budget, and then they have the nerve now, when they have been shamed into giving that money back, to claim credit for it.
Glen Bennett: It’s outrageous.
Hon KIERAN McANULTY: It is outrageous. Their record on health is outrageous. It is shameful. The facts speak for themselves. I would challenge any Government member to go and stand outside their local hospital, be it in Waikato or in Auckland City or in Middlemore or in Wairarapa or in Palmerston North or in Northland or in Nelson-Marlborough and to tell the truth—tell the facts: that their nursing numbers have gone backwards, and then tell people to vote for them. They won’t do it, will they?
Glen Bennett: No, they won’t.
Hon KIERAN McANULTY: They won’t, because they know that no one is going to vote for a Government that says it as it is, that tells the facts, that tells the truth that says despite three years in power, despite making all sorts of claims about expenditure in health, things have gotten worse. Fact: things have gone backwards—fact. They can’t spin their way out of it. They tried. They tried to mislead the country and they got caught out. But they don’t care—they don’t care.
: They think that they can win this election by misleading people. I’ll give you an example: the National Party want to sell Air New Zealand. They want to privatise our national carrier. Is that true? No. That’s what the ACT Party want to do. It would be dishonest for me to say that the National Party want to do something because their coalition wants to do something. But that is not what the National Party is doing, is it?
Glen Bennett: No.
Hon KIERAN McANULTY: No. They are not sticking to the truth; they are trying to collate things and present a problem. So if it is dishonest for me to say that the National Party want to sell Air New Zealand, it is dishonest for the National Party to say that the Labour Party want to introduce nine new taxes. They know it isn’t true, but they say it anyway.
: What does it say about a Government with a record of three years behind them that they have to make things up to make themselves look electable; that, after three years of being in Government, they have to go to New Zealand and say, “Vote for us because these guys are going to do nine new taxes.”, despite the fact they know it isn’t true. That’s hardly a record to stand on. That is why they’re doing it. They have hardly got a record to stand on so they have to make things up to make themselves look electable.
: I haven’t even mentioned New Zealand First; that speaks for itself. They’re going backwards; I’m going to leave them alone. They’re doing themselves damage; that’s fine by me. But the fact is that New Zealanders can see through this fib. They can see through the nonsense. They know that in their local hospitals, things are going backwards. If nurses aren’t allowed to be hired, they have been cut; if work needs to be done, the money’s been put elsewhere to fill the hole in their Budget.
: This is the reality that New Zealanders are facing: the highest homelessness in the history of this country.
Rima Nakhle: Not true.
Hon KIERAN McANULTY: The highest homelessness in the history of this country.
Rima Nakhle: According to who?
Hon KIERAN McANULTY: Rima Nakhle always changes seats in order to heckle—have you noticed that? It still doesn’t work. She says that it is not true. Well, I’ll tell you what? New Zealanders, here is a simple choice for you: who are you going to believe? Those people on the front lines, like the Wellington City Mission, the Auckland City Mission, the Christchurch City Mission, or the Methodist Mission, or Rima Nakhle? Who are New Zealanders going to believe? The people who are working with homelessness, the people who are working with our most vulnerable—those who say that it is the worst they have ever experienced, the worst that the country has ever seen—who are they going to believe? Them? The people who know what they’re not talking about? Or desperate National MPs who only have a matter of weeks left in the job who are clinging on to anything—making things up in order to stay in this job. I know who New Zealanders are going to believe: the ones who are actually telling the truth. They are ones who they are going to believe. In just over two months’ time, we’re going to see that in action.
TOM RUTHERFORD (National—Bay of Plenty): If there was ever a pitch for leadership on that side of the House, that was it—that was it. One of the prerequisites, as Suze Redmayne said, is he has to wear a tie. So that discounts half of his colleagues on that side, but that was the leadership pitch. And that was the leadership pitch after a 24 percent poll result in this week’s Roy Morgan Poll on that side for Labour: 24 percent. They’re taking a dive—they’re taking a deep dive. You just wait: the hospital pass will come in. Mr McAnulty, Chris Hipkins has read the tea leaves, and we think you should take it up, and take on the mantle.
: Ladies and gentlemen, he’ll use that speech, right there, to say, “Colleagues, I’m the white knight, I’m coming to save the day. Don’t worry about Wairarapa. Don’t worry about that. I want to lead this party and this country.” That’s what that speech was—that’s what that was. That was the leadership pitch. The only downside is he only had three other colleagues here to listen to it—and one of them is retiring, and he’s out of here; he’s checked out. He was yawning during that contribution; he was so bored—he was so bored. So there are no votes there. That was a leadership pitch if I’ve ever heard one.
Hon Kieran McAnulty: But you’ve seen two already this year.
TOM RUTHERFORD: But we’re actually here to talk about the Appropriation (2026/27 Estimates) Bill; that’s what we’re actually here to talk about. We’re not here to talk about things here, things there—
Hon Kieran McAnulty: Did you vote for Erica, or did you vote for “Bish”? It was Erica, wasn’t it? Or was it Penk?
TOM RUTHERFORD: We’re here to talk about the appropriation bill, Mr McAnulty.
Hon Kieran McAnulty: Who did you vote for? Was it Erica? It was Erica!
TOM RUTHERFORD: Well, I certainly didn’t vote for you, sir—I certainly didn’t vote for you. If I lived in the Wairarapa, my vote would have gone to Mike Butterick every day of the week—every day of the week, Mike Butterick. That’s a true representative, one that actually lives in his community; one that actually lives in it, and knows and lives and breathes it.
Hon Kieran McAnulty: Point of order. As everybody in this House knows, I love the hustle and bustle of this House, but it is inappropriate and unparliamentary to make an inaccurate claim about someone’s personal circumstances. I do live in Wairarapa and the member should not allude otherwise.
DEPUTY SPEAKER: Yes, I expect that Tom Rutherford would apologise to the member.
TOM RUTHERFORD: Madam Speaker, I withdraw and apologise.
DEPUTY SPEAKER: And I also want to remind the member that we’re on appropriations, and I know we’ve gone a bit political this afternoon, but a little bit of the appropriation bill in the speech would be good.
TOM RUTHERFORD: That’s great—I’ve got seven minutes and 42 seconds to do so.
: If we’re talking about accurate records in the House, there should be other members standing up and correcting the record at the same time. I just wonder, if the member on that side wants to hold that standard, maybe he should look across his benches to other members on that side of the House and hold them to the exact same standard, because if he wants to hold us to that standard, he should start in his own glasshouse—his own glasshouse—and set the standard there.
: This year’s Budget was focused on fixing the basics and building the future. If I think of my home in Tauranga and the wider Bay of Plenty, one of the things from this year’s Budget that I’m so proud of—so proud of—was the funding for the redevelopment of the Tauranga Hospital. Our city has grown exponentially over the last 25 to 30 years—we’ve grown massively; we’ve been one of New Zealand’s fastest-growing areas across the country.
: Our men and women on the front line, working day to day in our Tauranga Hospital, are working in a constrained environment. Many Governments have known about the issue; many Governments have known about it. They have seen the droves of people coming across the Kaimai Ranges into Tauranga and seeing what we have in our slice of paradise. People have seen it; they know what we have: beautiful beaches, amazing communities, pretty damn good representations from their local members as well. But our Tauranga Hospital has been pushed to its absolute limit.
: This year’s Budget had funding to upgrade it—finally, finally, it had funding for the redevelopment of the Tauranga Hospital. That is something I am so proud of us about, as a Government, that we are delivering. I know my colleague Sam Uffindell, the MP for Tauranga, would share the same thoughts as I would, because for many men and women across Tauranga and the wider Bay of Plenty, they want to know that if they turn up to their hospital, they can get the service they need from the incredible front-line healthcare workers but also that they are working in an environment and in facilities that are there to support them. So I’m really proud that we’re the Government delivering the redevelopment of the Tauranga Hospital.
: Another thing I’m incredibly proud of, for us, is supporting our Port of Tauranga and the fast-track legislation that we’ve got that will enable growth, not just for Tauranga but for New Zealand—for New Zealand. This is New Zealand’s largest export port in the country—in the country—and it’s been our Government’s fast-track legislation that has enabled things like the Port of Tauranga, numerous renewable projects, numerous housing projects to finally be delivered; to change this attitude of no into, finally, a yes. And that is a good thing.
: Roading and investment into infrastructure is massive for Tauranga and the Bay of Plenty, and this year’s Budget is building on that. We’ve got two roads of national significance: State Highway 29, Tauriko West, stage one, started under us—started under us. They talk; we deliver on this side. They talk, they consult, they put heaps of money into consultants. Remember “light fail”? Remember “light fail”? Not one metre of track actually delivered. This side, we came into Government, we said we would begin Tauriko West, State Highway 29 and it’s under way. That is a great thing, delivered through numerous Budgets, as us, as a Government.
: And then there’s the Takitimu North Link, stage one, that’s progressing exceptionally well; opening in less than two years’ time for our community, which will be great. Fast track delivered for stage two already. Stage two is going to continue, and that is great. That’s what a Government of action actually does and I’m really, really proud of that.
: This year’s Budget delivers on the investment into roading and infrastructure: nearly $7 billion in capital investment and about $60 billion of infrastructure investment over the next four years. That’s jobs—that’s what that is. That’s opportunity. That’s saying to New Zealanders that we’ve got plans for the future. We’re creating jobs, creating opportunity, investing in local economies, creating growth—that is how a Government grows the size of the pie. That’s how you grow the pie, and that’s what Mike Butterick talks about a lot. You don’t cut the pie up into so many small pieces and try to tax the hell out of it; you grow the pie. You want to solve the cost of living, you create more jobs, you build growth, you lift wages. That’s how you do it.
Hon Dr Duncan Webb: I can’t afford a pie.
TOM RUTHERFORD: That’s how you do it. And Duncan Webb, he can yell—he can yell—but the only reason he’s yelling is he’s looking for a job in two months’ time. He’s looking for one in two months’ time. [Bell rings]
DEPUTY SPEAKER: The bell is the Business Committee clock. That one’s about 30 seconds behind.
TOM RUTHERFORD: OK, Madam Speaker, that’s fine.
DEPUTY SPEAKER: Just to inform the speaker.
TOM RUTHERFORD: That’s fine. I think of other opportunities coming in our community and I think of what we’re doing in law and order. Law and order, for many locals in the Bay of Plenty—if I knock on doors in Pāpāmoa, Mount Maunganui, Welcome Bay, Maungatapu, or Ōhauiti, they say to me, “Gosh, I feel a lot safer now than I did 2½ years ago. Gosh, I feel so much safer if I go to Bayfair or the Crossing or into Tauranga Central than I did 2½ years ago. Thank goodness your Government has invested in law and order and getting rid of the sense of lawlessness that was taking over this country.” Remember ram raids? Down 85 percent under our Government. Gang patches? I haven’t seen one of those for nearly two years—I haven’t seen one of them for nearly two years. And Greg O’Connor, last night, in his valedictory statement, said that he absolutely loved the gang patch ban. That’s maybe why he’s going—that’s maybe why he’s going: down the back if you’ve got a differing view to the front bench.
: And just, finally, the one thing I keep hearing is, “Please, don’t bring in any new taxes.” You want to do something about the cost of living, don’t take more of people’s own money; they’ve worked hard for it. You don’t grow this economy by digging into other people’s pockets; you do it by creating opportunities, creating a brighter future, focusing on the things that actually matter, and fixing the basics and building the future.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: The bills are set down for second reading, and the reports are set down for consideration. No bills have been introduced. The House comes to oral questions.
Oral Questions to Ministers
Local Government
Question No. 1

content.speaker: MIKE DAVIDSON (Green)
content.text: to the Minister of Local Government: Has he received any advice that shows that the rates cap will result in no savings for some households?

content.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS (Minister of Local Government)
content.text: I’ve received advice that the amount an average household saves will depend on what their council would otherwise have increased rates by, and how these rates are allocated. If a council is already close to or within the cap, the average savings will, naturally, be modest. That shows that the cap is workable when councils prioritise. But many ratepayers are facing double-digit increases. For example, under Hamilton City Council’s 2024 to 2034 long-term plan, an average household was on track to pay around $6,400 a year by 2034. With increases limited to 4 percent, that would be around $4,170, saving about $15,800 over a 10-year period. That is meaningful savings.

content.speaker: Mike Davidson
content.text: Does he think a young family saving $34 a year under the rates cap would be better or worse off once higher fees for pools, libraries, public transport, and car-parking are included, given his view in a Cabinet paper that a rates cap will “incentivise greater use of user charges”?

content.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS
content.text: First and foremost, I encourage the member to—[Interruption]

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Just hold on—wait on. We’ll start that again.

content.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. First and foremost, I’d encourage the member to read the bill in regards to rates capping. The cumulative effect of rates increases means that over a five- or 10-year period, Kiwi households will have considerable savings as a result of that cumulative effect being limited to 4 percent. Don’t forget the rates increases last year were 14 percent on average across New Zealand; this year, 9 percent—4 percent with respect to savings. What I also reflect is that not having a cap will not protect Kiwi ratepayers. Not having a cap will also not protect them against those double-digit rate increases, and that is not the policy of this Government.

content.speaker: Mike Davidson
content.text: How does he reconcile his claim that households will save money, with the Ministry for the Environment’s feedback that “reduced rates revenue may be offset by increased fees for services such as swimming pool entry, library fines, and parking. This could result in no net savings for many households.”?

content.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS
content.text: Well, on this side of the House, we understand the concept of prioritisation and making decisions in regards to spending that is within a limit. We don’t have a credit card without a limit on this side of the House, by any stretch. Councils will, and should, prioritise their spending, like every single Kiwi household and business in this country. I make no apology for councils needing to do that. Putting a limit on their increase of expenditure is a sensible and pragmatic thing to do to protect Kiwi households.

content.speaker: Mike Davidson
content.text: Does he accept that including water services investment, which is exempt from the rates cap, in his figures for Waitaki District Council in his answer to oral questions on 25 August artificially inflated his claims of savings by nearly 80 percent?

content.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS
content.text: No, because what I was providing there was an example of how much an average bill would increase—the differential between the average of 14 percent or 9 percent versus 4 percent. Basic maths would indicate to the member that when you increase cumulative bills by 14 percent or 9 percent, it is a heck of a lot bigger over a period of five or 10 years than at 4 percent. On this side of the House, we are on the side of Kiwi ratepayers. We want to protect Kiwi ratepayers from unreasonable, rollercoaster rates increases. That’s what we’re doing; we make no apologies for that. That side of the House has no plan to protect Kiwi ratepayers.

content.speaker: Mike Davidson
content.text: Is it correct that the biggest savings from his rates cap will go to owners of multimillion-dollar houses and holiday homes who don’t need support, while struggling families may only save as little as $34 a year, only to face higher costs from reduced local services?

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: A concise answer would be good.

content.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS
content.text: No.
Revenue
Question No. 2

content.speaker: DAN BIDOIS (National—Northcote)
content.text: to the Minister of Revenue: Is the Government considering a capital gains tax on properties used for both residential and business purposes?

content.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS (Minister of Revenue)
content.text: No, this Government will not introduce a capital gains tax on the family home or on small businesses. For many Kiwis, the line between the two isn’t so simple. They might live in the front of a property and run their business from a workshop, garage, or an office out the back. We won’t punish people for using their own homes to build a business and get ahead. We’re on the side of Kiwis that work hard, doing the right thing and wanting to get ahead.

content.speaker: Dan Bidois
content.text: Why do some New Zealanders choose to operate their business from the same property they live in?

content.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS
content.text: Because, for many small-business owners, it is the most practical and affordable way for them to operate. A builder, for example, might keep their tools and equipment at home. A mechanic might have a workshop on their property, or an entrepreneur couple might lease out their house as an airbnb during the summer break. These are ordinary Kiwis, using what they have to build something for themselves and their family.

content.speaker: Dan Bidois
content.text: What could a capital gains tax mean for a tradie or other small-business owner who operates their business from their family property?

content.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS
content.text: It could mean being taxed 28 percent on part of their family property, simply because they have used it to earn a living. That means that a Kiwi who has worked hard, paid their mortgage, and built a business from home could face a big tax bill when they sell or are due to retire. That is the wrong message. It punishes aspiration, rather than rewarding it. On this side of the House, we back people who work hard, invest, and take risks, and we do that and we say: no new taxes.
Social Development and Employment
Question No. 3

content.speaker: Hon CARMEL SEPULONI (Deputy Leader—Labour)
content.text: to the Minister for Social Development and Employment: Does she stand by all her statements and actions?

content.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON (Minister for Social Development and Employment)
content.text: Yes, in the context in which they were given.

content.speaker: Hon Carmel Sepuloni
content.text: Why, when 36,000 fifteen- to nineteen-year-olds are not in work, education, or training, did she cut the access to jobseeker payments of 18- and 19-year-olds?

content.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
content.text: Because our Government is clear: we want 18- and 19-year-olds in education, training, or employment, and if they’re not, we expect that their families do support them. We know that going on welfare is a trap. If a young person goes onto the jobseeker benefit under the age of 20, on average they will spend another 21 years of their life on welfare. Our side of the House is more aspirational for young people, and wants more for their futures.

content.speaker: Hon Carmel Sepuloni
content.text: How can she say she is supporting young people into work, when in this term, she has cut off their access to a benefit while also limiting non-beneficiaries’ access to employment support programmes?

content.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
content.text: I refute that. We now have 4,000 young people in job coaching, which is a very intensive programme. We’re also incentivising those young people who then go into employment and stay in a job for 12 months with a $1,000 bonus. We are doing things differently. We want to release young people from the trap that they would otherwise fall into if those guys were still in office. We want more for them.

content.speaker: Hon Carmel Sepuloni
content.text: How can she deny that she has moved the goalposts for young people accessing Ministry of Social Development (MSD) employment programmes, when programmes like Mana in Mahi, Flexi-wage, and the Mayors Taskforce for Jobs are almost entirely only available to those on benefit under her watch?

content.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
content.text: As I said, we have higher aspirations for the other side in terms of young people. They have access to He Poutama Rangatahi; they have access to the Limited Service Volunteer, one of the most successful programmes we have. Intensive job coaching. There are now 70,000 New Zealanders in job coaching and case management. Case management is the most effective intervention that MSD offers. We want more for young people, and we’ll never apologise for that.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Just a reminder to the interjectors there: I didn’t cut anything off, although I’m tempted.

content.speaker: Hon Carmel Sepuloni
content.text: Has she been advised if the Ministry of Social Development is recommending that young people approaching them for help, who can no longer receive a benefit or get access to effective MSD employment programmes, should go and get a credit card?

content.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
content.text: No. We clearly want young people to be in education, in training, in employment. That’s why in Budget 2026 we’ve invested more in Youth Guarantee, and in an additional 10,000 places in trades training. We want to see young people get ahead in life, and that’s why we are changing the settings to ensure that they have that opportunity.

content.speaker: Hon Carmel Sepuloni
content.text: Is it the Minister’s view that it is better for a young person to owe money on a credit card than to receive help from the Ministry of Social Development?

content.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
content.text: As I said at the start, we believe that young people should be in employment, education, or training, or supported by their families. If you look at comparable countries, in Australia, there is a parental income test up to the age of 22; in France, you’ve got no access to welfare under the age of 25. This is a balanced approach—

content.speaker: Hon Willow-Jean Prime
content.text: This is New Zealand. You’re the Minister in New Zealand.

content.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
content.text: Well, we normally compare ourselves to Australia. I’ve just said it’s up to the age of 22, and, as I said, our side of the House is more aspirational for young people than allowing them to get stuck on welfare, where they stay another 21 years of their life—21 years. It’s got to be better than that. [Interruption]

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Good, that’s enough. Just completely calm down.

content.speaker: Dr Tracey McLellan
content.text: You’re just making it up now.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: I beg your pardon?

content.speaker: Hon Carmel Sepuloni
content.text: Why does she refuse to acknowledge that at a time of rising unemployment and job losses, she has actively made it harder for young people to get into work by restricting access to the very programmes designed to help them and has cut them off from getting welfare support, and how can young people possibly afford another three years of a National Government?

content.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
content.text: Very simply: because our side of the House knows that growing the economy grows employment opportunities; 220,000 is the Treasury forecast. A job for a young person is a better life, a better future, and we’re going to stick with that every day of the week, because we’re fixing the basics, and building the future for young New Zealanders. [Interruption]

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: That general barrage like that has to stop. It’s the last question like that.
Revenue
Question No. 4

content.speaker: SUZE REDMAYNE (National—Rangitīkei)
content.text: to the Minister of Revenue: Is the Government considering introducing an inheritance or gift tax?

content.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS (Minister of Revenue)
content.text: No, this Government will not introduce an inheritance or gift tax. New Zealanders work hard, save, and invest so that they can build a better future for themselves and their families. This Government backs aspiration, and we will not be waiting at the end with another tax. [Interruption]

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Just a moment. I made the point before that when a question is being asked, no one else speaks, and when a Minister is answering a question, he doesn’t need his colleagues to assist him—or her.

content.speaker: Suze Redmayne
content.text: What types of New Zealanders could be affected by an inheritance or gift tax?

content.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS
content.text: All New Zealanders who have worked hard will build up assets over their lifetime. An inheritance tax could tax a home; a small business; people with a farm, savings, investments, or other assets they want to pass on to their children. These are everyday New Zealanders who have spent decades building something up for themselves and their families. In what may already be one of the hardest moments in someone’s life—having just lost a parent or a loved one—the last thing a family should face is an inheritance tax bill from the Government.

content.speaker: Suze Redmayne
content.text: What impact could an inheritance or gift tax have on New Zealanders’ incentives to save, invest, and build something for the next generation? [Interruption]

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Is somebody else wanting to answer the question?

content.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS
content.text: It sends a chilling message to hard-working Kiwis. Instead, on this side of the House, we want New Zealanders to save, to invest, to build businesses and create wealth for themselves and their children. Layering new taxes on people who do these things would discourage investment, hold back growth, and make it harder for Kiwi families to get ahead. That is not what we stand for on this side of the House. Our focus is on fixing the basics, building the future, and no new taxes.
RMA Reform
Question No. 5

content.speaker: Hon WILLIE JACKSON (Labour)
content.text: to the Minister responsible for RMA Reform: Does he stand by his statement that “it's absolutely paramount for this Government that we protect settlements that have been entered into in good faith”; if not, why?

content.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice)
content.text: on behalf of the Minister responsible for RMA Reform: Yes.

content.speaker: Hon Willie Jackson
content.text: How is overriding the Environment Court, which ruled earlier this year that plan change 1 (PC 1) must remain central to protecting the Waikato and Waipā rivers, acting in good faith with iwi?

content.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH
content.text: Well, on behalf of the Minister, the Government’s decision to pause PC1 is a practical measure to support the transition to the new planning system. PC1 arrives at the very moment our new planning system is replacing the Resource Management Act (RMA), and we don’t want farmers and growers to incur the costs in transitioning into PC1’s farmer environmental plan and consent framework, which will soon be replaced by others.

content.speaker: Hon Willie Jackson
content.text: Can the Minister explain why Waikato-Tainui, Raukawa, Ngāti Maniapoto, Te Arawa, and Tūwharetoa jointly wrote to him warning that his delay would be a direct breach, and can he tell this House which one of those five iwi he decided to listen to before ignoring all of them?

content.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH
content.text: Well, on behalf of the Minister, I certainly did not ignore them. We met with iwi multiple times, as did officials. The proposal does not change the Government’s commitment to upholding Treaty settlements, including Te Ture Whaimana o te Awa o Waikato. No settlement says we could never change the planning system, and so what we’re working on is adjusting that arrangement for the new system.

content.speaker: Hon Willie Jackson
content.text: Does he agree with Tukoroirangi Morgan that the Government has “step[ped] in to override judicial directions at the behest of their political donors”, and is that another example of good faith?

content.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH
content.text: On behalf of the Minister, no, I don’t agree with that statement.

content.speaker: Hon Willie Jackson
content.text: Will he attend Koroneihana to discuss why, at the start of his own RMA reforms, plan changes giving effect to Treaty settlements—including PC1—would continue, and then break that commitment three months later without the agreement of any of the five iwi affected, and if not, why?

content.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH
content.text: On behalf of the Minister, I’m not sure of my travel plans, but I do know that my excellent colleagues, Ministers Potaka and Goldsmith, will be attending.
Social Development and Employment
Question No. 6

content.speaker: RICARDO MENÉNDEZ MARCH (Green)
content.text: to the Minister for Social Development and Employment: What are the terms of reference, if any, of the review of the wrongful benefit suspensions, and will the review consider compensation?

content.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON (Minister for Social Development and Employment)
content.text: I have made it clear to the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) that the review will consider the winter energy payment issue and processing delays. The review will cover what has occurred and who has been affected in operationalising mandatory reviews and any further actions that may be needed to prevent these issues happening again. As I’ve already made clear in the House, I will wait for the findings of the review on 10 September.

content.speaker: Ricardo Menéndez March
content.text: Does she acknowledge that supported living payment recipients were captured by mandatory reviews, which ended up leading to processing delays, meaning that they live often week to week without any savings; and, if so, does she accept that even a week’s worth of missed payments could push people into hardship, hunger, or homelessness?

content.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
content.text: As I’ve already said, the suspension of payments that was made incorrectly will have had an impact on New Zealanders, and I accept that that would have been challenging for many, which is why I had asked MSD to focus with urgency on making sure that those payments were reinstated and backdated at pace.

content.speaker: Ricardo Menéndez March
content.text: If she recognises the impact this could have had on people, including people being left hungry, potentially homeless, or in hardship, why is she not commenting on the possibility of compensation?

content.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
content.text: Well, as I’ve said, I will wait for the findings of the review.

content.speaker: Ricardo Menéndez March
content.text: What is the point of an apology if she’s not even willing to consider the option of compensation for harm that may have occurred and which is not redressed through back payments, as that cannot make up for potential debt or harm or worsening health outcomes that people may have experienced due to missed payments?

content.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
content.text: As I said, the review will cover many components, including who has been affected, and that’s why I’m waiting for that review.
Tourism and Hospitality
Question No. 7

content.speaker: CATHERINE WEDD (National—Tukituki)
content.text: to the Minister for Tourism and Hospitality: What recent progress has she seen on tourism in New Zealand?

content.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON (Minister for Tourism and Hospitality)
content.text: Recent data from Statistics New Zealand shows New Zealand’s international visitor numbers continue to climb. Over 201,000 international visitors arrived in New Zealand in June 2026, which is up 8.1 percent on June 2025. That puts international visitor arrivals for June at 95 percent of the 2019 levels for the same period. Growing tourism is a key part of our Government’s plan to fix the basics and build the future. This progress shows that our plan to grow the economy is working.

content.speaker: Catherine Wedd
content.text: What markets are seeing the strongest growth?

content.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
content.text: We are seeing continued growth from our largest visitor market—Australia—with 108,200 arrivals, which is up 14 percent from last June. There was also strong growth from other key tourism markets, including from China, with visitor arrivals reaching 14,300, which is up 27 percent compared to June last year. Close to 200,000 cruise ship passengers are also expected to arrive in New Zealand this season, with the launch at the weekend of the cruise season. We are seeing the flow on of growth and confidence in our tourism and hospitality sector as more visitors choose New Zealand as their next holiday destination.

content.speaker: Catherine Wedd
content.text: What steps is the Government taking to support progress in tourism growth?

content.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
content.text: We know domestic visitors generate nearly twice as many guest nights as international visitors and account for around two-thirds of all guest nights across New Zealand. We do not believe that New Zealanders booking a weekend away or travelling for a family funeral, or a sports team travelling for a game should face an additional tax on top of the costs they already pay when travelling domestically. That’s why we don’t believe in a bed tax and we are working hard to attract more tourists to New Zealand, because the more visitors we have in our cities and regions, the more money is being spent in shops and cafes. It’s a key part of our plan to grow the economy so that we can keep investing in the front-line public services Kiwis rely on, without having to reach for new taxes.
Health
Question No. 8

content.speaker: Hon Dr AYESHA VERRALL (Labour)
content.text: to the Minister of Health: Does he stand by his statement that “A sustainable health system relies on a steady pipeline of skilled New Zealand-trained nurses entering the workforce”; if so, why?

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY (Associate Minister of Health)
content.text: on behalf of the Minister of Health: Yes, in the context it was made. As the member will be aware, more than 2,100 additional nurses, on a net basis, have been employed by Health New Zealand since 2023, which equates to a net increase of 1,640 fulltime-equivalents. The Government remains focused on building on this track record so that we can continue to reduce wait times for patients and build the future of our healthcare system. That is why, as at 14 August, there were 2,378 fulltime-equivalent nursing roles actively being recruited across Health New Zealand, including 475 nurses who have accepted offers, with thousands more progressing through recruitment.

content.speaker: Tangi Utikere
content.text: Why have emergency department staff in Palmerston North had to resort to begging Health New Zealand to send urgent help after he cut the number of nurses by 25 over the past two years?

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY
content.text: Well, clearly, from my primary answer, that is incorrect, and what I would point to is putting a wrecking ball to the health system in the middle of a pandemic, centralising the health system, and taking away local decision-making. That member’s question reinforces why, on 1 July, we brought back local decision-making for budgets, service delivery, and recruitment decisions.

content.speaker: Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall
content.text: Supplementary. [Interruption]

content.speaker: Hon Kieran McAnulty
content.text: Point of order, sir.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: No, just a moment. You can’t just—OK, point of order, the Hon Kieran McAnulty.

content.speaker: Hon Kieran McAnulty
content.text: Point of order, Mr Speaker. I’m just seeking clarity from you as to the process. When a Minister makes an incorrect statement on behalf of another Minister, which Minister is required to correct that statement in the House?

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Then it would be, presumably, the Minister on whose behalf the mistake has been made. Can I just say I could hear some of these things better if there wasn’t quite so much interjection.

content.speaker: Hon Jo Luxton
content.text: Why, when emergency department (ED) nurses are having to strike for safe staffing at Gisborne Hospital, has he hired just two additional nurses across the entire district in the last year?

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY
content.text: On behalf of the health Minister, it is not for the Labour Party or the unions to decide safe staffing levels; it’s a clinical decision by Health New Zealand, and the advice I’ve got is 75 percent of shifts have been on or above target.

content.speaker: Cushla Tangaere-Manuel
content.text: Why isn’t he taking action to raise the number of Māori nurses when only 7 percent of nurses are Māori and Māori experience worse health outcomes?

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY
content.text: On behalf of the Minister, I would like to point to the great work of the mental health Minister, with the mental health commission in its latest report pointing to the increased diversity in our health workforce, specifically our nursing health workforce.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: The Hon Phil Twyford—and nobody else.

content.speaker: Hon Phil Twyford
content.text: Why, when stroke patients at Waitakere Hospital’s Muriwai ward are left languishing in wet beds and at risk of falls due to lack of nurses, has he only hired 54 nurses across New Zealand in the last two years?

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY
content.text: On behalf of the Minister, I won’t take any crocodile tears from the Opposition, because when they were in Government, nursing vacancies topped at 2,632. As of March 2026, they’re down to 1,600. The vacancy rate, 8.6 percent for nurses, is now down to 5.2 percent. We are delivering.

content.speaker: Rachel Boyack
content.text: Supplementary.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Yep—

content.speaker: Rachel Boyack
content.text: Rachel Boyack.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: —Rachel Boyack.

content.speaker: Rachel Boyack
content.text: Why, when he has cut the number of nurses in the top of the South by 30 fulltime-equivalents in the past year alone, are nurses being forced to pick and choose which patients get care each day?

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY
content.text: On behalf of the health Minister, you only need to refer to my primary answer that shows that, actually, the trend line shows that we have employed not only more nurses, but when you look at the numbers that we’ll offer employment to 1,800 graduate nurses, that is the biggest offer in any year of the last seven years.

content.speaker: Shanan Halbert
content.text: Why, when North Shore ED nurses have declared a state of emergency due to a critical lack of staff, which has left elderly patients in soiled beds, has he failed to properly staff North Shore Hospital?

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY
content.text: On behalf of the health Minister, that is the very reason why we have recruited more nurses into roles to drive down vacancy rates. That is the very reason why we have funded more into winter preparedness plans. That is the very reason why this Government is the first Government to deliver an online 24/7 primary care service to take the pressure off ED.

content.speaker: Lemauga Lydia Sosene
content.text: When he has cut the number of nurses at Middlemore Hospital by 74 over the past two years, is it any wonder that nurses are saying, “We’re sinking quite quickly because people are so sick.”?

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY
content.text: On behalf of the health Minister, what I say nurses are saying through the turnover rate is under their watch it was 11.7 percent; now it’s down to 8.4 percent. Nurses are saying they’re staying.

content.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
content.text: Could the Minister tell us, during the massive nurse shortages by 2023, how many of those questioners were asking questions in Parliament about that?

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY
content.text: On behalf of—

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: No, you don’t have responsibility for a previous Parliament.

content.speaker: Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall
content.text: Why, when hospitals across New Zealand are in urgent need of nurses, will he not commit to offering every New Zealand trained nurse a job?

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY
content.text: On behalf of the Minister of Health, what a reckless policy, to spend half a billion dollars on committed funding already in the health system. That member needs to come clean. What will she cut to pay for it—

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: No, no—stop. You’re going to address the question, not start with an attack. Please address the question—or ask the question again.

content.speaker: Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall
content.text: Why, when hospitals across New Zealand are in urgent need of more nurses, will he not commit to offering every New Zealand-trained nurse a job?

content.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY
content.text: On behalf of the Minister, it’s amazing how everything seems so easy when you’re in Opposition and do very little in Government. The figures I’ve said today, of offering to 1,800 graduate nurses, is the biggest offer in this country out of any year for the last seven years. We’re committed to growing the workforce. That is why vacancy rates have come down, turnover rates have come down, but most of all, there are 2,100 more nurses at the front lines of our health system.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: I’ve taken further advice from the point of order raised by the Hon Kieran McAnulty before. I’m advised that because members are responsible only for their own statements in the House, the Minister answering on behalf would be responsible for correcting incorrect statements.
Small Business and Manufacturing
Question No. 9

content.speaker: GRANT McCALLUM (National—Northland)
content.text: to the Minister for Small Business and Manufacturing: Does the Government have any plans to introduce a capital gains tax on small businesses?

content.speaker: Hon CAMERON BREWER (Minister for Small Business and Manufacturing)
content.text: No. The Government has no such plans. My focus as Minister for Small Business and Manufacturing is on lowering costs for businesses and backing the nearly 600,000 small businesses in New Zealand to grow and succeed. Taxing owners on the premises that they have spent a lifetime building would do the opposite. This Government backs the people who take the risk and build something.

content.speaker: Grant McCallum
content.text: What has the Minister heard from small-business owners about what happens to property that they operate from when they sell up?

content.speaker: Hon CAMERON BREWER
content.text: What I hear constantly is that the two cannot be separated. If the member was to look on what he would call his “TradeMe machine”, what he would see today, for sale, is a mechanic in the Hutt, a pub in Hokitika, a motorbike dealer in Ngātea—businesses and building sold as one. For those owners, that building is their retirement plan. If the workshop’s value rises by $100,000, a capital gains tax, at 28 percent, takes $28,000 off it. A tax on the shop floor is a tax on their hard-earned retirement.

content.speaker: Grant McCallum
content.text: How would such a capital gains tax affect owners who face selling up not by choice but because of ill-health or a relationship breakdown?

content.speaker: Hon CAMERON BREWER
content.text: It would hit them at the worst possible moment. These things cannot be planned: a diagnosis arrives, a marriage ends, and an owner shuts up shop and has to take whatever the sale brings. They are not selling at the top of the market; they are selling because they have to. A capital gains tax on top of that is just, frankly, salt in the wound. Taxing someone on the way out is not taxing success; it is taxing bad luck.
Tertiary Education
Question No. 10

content.speaker: SHANAN HALBERT
content.text: How many people were there in work-based learning last year, and how does that compare to the number of people in work-based learning in 2023?

content.speaker: Hon PENNY SIMMONDS
content.text: Point of order, Mr Speaker. I’m wondering if the person asking the question might like to read from the actual question that he put.

content.speaker: SHANAN HALBERT (Labour)
content.text: to the Minister for Tertiary Education: How many people were there in work-based learning last year, and how does that compare to the number of people in work-based learning in 2023?

content.speaker: Hon PENNY SIMMONDS
content.text: Mr Speaker, would he like to try another go at it?

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: No, he wouldn’t, and it might be a good idea to take a view that the Leader of the House would want things to be moving along, I’m sure, quite speedily given the debate that’s coming.

content.speaker: Hon PENNY SIMMONDS (Minister for Tertiary Education)
content.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. There were 138,730 learners in work-based learning in 2023, and 108,315 learners in 2025. This decline in apprentice numbers reflects lower levels of business confidence that we inherited from the previous Government, driven by higher costs and economic pressures, particularly in the construction sector. The good news is that recent Treasury forecasts predict 220,000 more jobs being created over the next four years, so we expect to see apprentice numbers track up as businesses feel more confident in training new staff—as long as they haven’t got to face nine new taxes.

content.speaker: Shanan Halbert
content.text: Is it correct that the number of apprentices has dropped to a 15-year low under her watch?

content.speaker: Hon PENNY SIMMONDS
content.text: Well, as I said before, it was an economic situation that we inherited. What I can say, though, is that the previous number of apprentices through Apprenticeship Boost were not actually completing their qualifications, so there was a significant decline in credit-completion rates: in 2021, 67 percent only; in 2025, 86 percent credit-completion rates. Apprentice retention rates have increased under this Government and attrition rates have decreased. That is a better outcome.

content.speaker: Shanan Halbert
content.text: Does she agree with Building and Construction Industry Training Organisation (BCITO) chief executive Jason Hungerford, who said, “We’ve got around 600 people ready and willing to start an apprenticeship right now. What we don’t have is perhaps the confidence in some of those employers that are willing to take that next step and take them on.”?

content.speaker: Hon PENNY SIMMONDS
content.text: I agree with Jason Hungerford BCITO CEO when he said, “There are signs that building and construction are starting to recover, and that should result in more apprentices and workplace training.”

content.speaker: Shanan Halbert
content.text: Does she agree with Energy and Infrastructure Industry Skills Board chief executive, Philip Aldridge, who said that a lack of apprentices means “we’re going to have difficulty resourcing up for key initiatives, whether it’s roading, water, extractive projects”?

content.speaker: Hon PENNY SIMMONDS
content.text: I agree with the Manufacturing and Engineering Industry Skills Board, which says manufacturing companies are intending to increase apprentice numbers: “Apprentice numbers have generally been subdued for a few years as we’ve come off a post-COVID high and business confidence being hit by the extended war in the Gulf. However, our manufacturing and engineering industries have been continuing, with signs of recovery and growth over the last year, and many companies now face skill shortages and consequently are looking to take on more apprentices.”

content.speaker: Shanan Halbert
content.text: Is she surprised that her plan of “cut, cut, disestablish, cut” has led to a drop in apprenticeship numbers and will leave key industries struggling for workers?

content.speaker: Hon PENNY SIMMONDS
content.text: As I’ve said before, it’s very difficult to cut a budget that wasn’t there, and there was no budget for Apprenticeship Boost from the end of 2024. This Government rescued Apprenticeship Boost and targeted Apprenticeship Boost, and therefore, we are delighted to see that so many industries are intending to take on more apprentices as the economy grows. It is why we are so focused on growing the economy, not adding more taxes.
Food Safety
Question No. 11

content.speaker: CAMERON LUXTON (ACT)
content.text: to the Minister for Food Safety: What recent announcements has he made about reducing barriers to New Zealanders accessing home-kill and hunted meats?

content.speaker: Hon ANDREW HOGGARD (Minister for Food Safety)
content.text: This week, I announced that the Government is consulting on the rules for home-kill and hunted meat, including the 28-day rule. This rule means that if you buy, or are given, an animal off a local farmer, a listed home-kill provider cannot process it for you until you’ve shown that you’ve been caring for it for 28 days. No one has looked at these rules in 20 years, and this consultation is part of a sustained Government effort to reduce red tape and bring the cost of good quality food down for consumers.

content.speaker: Cameron Luxton
content.text: Why does the Minster believe the 28-day rule needs looking at?

content.speaker: Hon ANDREW HOGGARD
content.text: If a neighbour or a close friend wants to come to my farm and I’m prepared to sell or even give them—probably not give them—a lamb or a beast for the freezer, then I can’t see why the Government would stand in the way of that. Not only does it give people access to more affordable food, but it also supports thriving and more connected rural communities. This consultation will be about testing whether there genuinely is a food safety need for this rule or whether it’s just an example of a silly rule that’s just standing in the way of unlocking New Zealand’s potential.

content.speaker: Cameron Luxton
content.text: What impact would this change have on food prices?

content.speaker: Hon ANDREW HOGGARD
content.text: I can’t be concrete in my numbers, but my experience as a farmer, sending animals to the works, is that you get paid a lot less for that animal than if you were to go and buy it piece by piece in the supermarket. Being able to supply meat, this animal, directly to people will leave that difference in their back pocket.

content.speaker: Cameron Luxton
content.text: What has the Minister heard from farmers and hunters about donating meat?

content.speaker: Hon ANDREW HOGGARD
content.text: I’ve heard from hunters and farmers who want to give meat to local sports clubs, community organisations, or food banks and aren’t sure if they’re allowed to. There are ways to donate, but there does appear to be some inconsistency in different pieces of legislation, which is driving uncertainty among people who want to help. Meat is the number one thing food banks are looking for, and the dearest thing for them to provide. That’s a waste on both sides, and it’s worth cleaning up.

content.speaker: SPEAKER
content.text: Do you take cash for those cattle beasts, or how does it work?

content.speaker: Hon ANDREW HOGGARD
content.text: With the GST. I don’t want to upset the revenue Minister.
Justice
Question No. 12

content.speaker: CELIA WADE-BROWN (Green)
content.text: to the Minister of Justice: What actions, if any, has his Government taken to lift voter enrolment among 18- to 24-year-olds?

content.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice)
content.text: I’m advised that $18.1 million has been allocated by the Electoral Commission to support enrolment in the 2026 election, after the Government provided an additional $61.8 million in the Budget 2025 to support the effectiveness and timeliness of electoral services. That $18 million compares with $10.8 million in the previous election. The Electoral Commission, I note, of course, is independent and is undertaking a significant, nationwide information and education programme, which will help young people and first-time voters know how to enrol. I’m sure every New Zealander will have seen all the various notices around town.

content.speaker: Celia Wade-Brown
content.text: What is he doing to ensure the Electoral Commission’s outreach to rangatahi is effective, given enrolment among 18- to 24-year-olds is just 57.5 percent and significantly lower than at the same time in the last election?

content.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH
content.text: I’ll give the member the latest figures: yes, overall, enrolment is at 89.7 percent, compared with 88.7 percent three years ago. So we’re actually ahead, but it’s true that when it comes to young people, it’s currently 56.9 percent, compared with 59.7 percent, so we’re two points below where we were. My encouragement to the Electoral Commission and to the young people of New Zealand will be to get themselves enrolled as quickly as possible. That is why we’ve put some extra resources into the hands of the Electoral Commission, but I do note they are being very energetic in their efforts to get people enrolled.

content.speaker: Celia Wade-Brown
content.text: Why is he making it harder to vote during the 13-day pre-election period, the exact period when, last election, about 50,000 young people enrolled to vote?

content.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH
content.text: Well, that 50,000 enrolled to vote during that period last time because they could; but this time, they won’t be able to, and we’ve been sending a very clear message for a very long time now that the rules have changed. We’ve done that because we were facing an ever-increasing number of special votes, and special votes take 10 times as long to deal with after the election. I encourage young people to tune in. For example, as well as advertising in news media and in in-person community events and digital social channels that are being used, the Electoral Commission is also advertising on channels that young people use—in particular, Snapchat, TikTok—and they’re even advertising on gaming platforms, so thorough is their effort to ensure that people have every opportunity to get enrolled. But I would remind people that are tuning in and listening to this that it is a requirement under the law, if you are 18, to be enrolled. And so get yourself enrolled—it’s not hard—and then you can vote.

content.speaker: Celia Wade-Brown
content.text: What does he say to young people in Ōtāhuhu and Manurewa where fewer than 42 percent of eligible 18- to 24-year-olds are enrolled?

content.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH
content.text: My message to the young people of Ōtāhuhu is get enrolled. It’s not hard to do, and if you want to vote, you should get yourself enrolled. My advice to them, of course, would be to party vote National.

Appropriation (2026/27 Estimates) Bill
Imprest Supply (Second for 2026/27) Bill
Third Reading and Second Reading

content.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS (Minister of Revenue)
content.text: on behalf of the Minister of Finance: I move, That the Appropriation (2026/27 Estimates) Bill be now read a third time and the Imprest Supply (Second for 2026/27) Bill be now read a second time.

These two bills before the House today are both very important to our public finance system. Appropriation bills and imprest supply bills give the Government the authorisation by Parliament to spend money lawfully. The Public Finance Act makes it clear that the Government cannot incur expenses or commit capital expenditure without that authority. This is the constitutional principle long since held since the restoration of the Crown in the United Kingdom in 1660. For members and those listening at home, more detail on the history of the imprest supply can be found in chapter 42 of McGee.

The Imprest Supply (Second for 2026/27) Bill provides interim parliamentary authority for expenditure decisions made or to be made by the Government through to the end of the financial year that are additional to the amounts in the 2026-27 Estimates. The second imprest bill provides for any operating or capital decisions, including precommitments against future Budget allowances and expenditure incurred against the between-Budget contingency. It also covers fiscally neutral adjustments which increase one appropriation but decrease another, confirmation of expense transfers, increases in demand-driven appropriations, and drawdowns of existing tagged contingencies. Provisions are also made for any risks that may materialise—for example, matters covered in the “Risks to the Forecasts” chapter of the Budget Economic and Fiscal Update.

The amount of authority requested in the Imprest Supply (Second for 2026/27) Bill is $29 billion, made up of $16 billion of expenses, $12 billion of capital expenditure, and $1 billion of capital injections. The amount requested this year is broadly consistent with those sought in recent years’ second imprest supply bills, except for last year. The significantly higher amount requested last year reflected a provision for the potential one-off transfer of approximately $30 billion of school property assets from the Ministry of Education to the New Zealand School Property Agency. The amount sought in this imprest bill will be sufficient to cover any expenditure that may be incurred in this financial year that is additional to what is in the 2026-27 Estimates.

Treasury reporting indicates that actual expenditures incurred against imprest supply Acts are considerably lower than the authority provided by legislation. All expenditure incurred under the interim authority of the second imprest supply bill still needs to be appropriated by Parliament before the end of the financial year, as is the case every year. This will be done through the Appropriation (2026/27 Supplementary Estimates) Bill, which will be introduced on Budget day 2027.

Not only do we have before us the second imprest supply bill, but we also debate the third reading of the Appropriation (2026/27 Estimates) Bill, which had its second reading on Budget day, 28 May 2026. This bill sees the Budget becoming law—a Budget that is focused on securing New Zealand’s future. Budget 2026 is a responsible Budget that boosts funding for essential services and invests in the infrastructure New Zealanders need for the future without breaking the bank.

Thanks to this Government’s careful management of the public finances, New Zealand is digging its way out of the post-COVID fiscal and economic hole. Balanced books are now in sight, with a forecast return to surplus in 2028-29. Returning to surplus and reducing debt means that more of the tax dollars earned by hard-working New Zealanders can be invested in the front-line services and infrastructure Kiwis rely on rather than servicing interest costs. We are building the future through Budget 2026, with investment in State highways, rail, hospitals, schools, social housing, courthouses, police stations, and defence capability. These investments mean thousands of jobs up and down the country, improved transport connections, and support for economic growth.

There are a few key announcements from Budget 2026 that I want to draw to the attention of the House this afternoon. The single biggest item in the Budget is support for front-line health services. Next year, Government spending on the health system is expected to total $34 billion, which equates to $17,000 for every New Zealand household. Budget 2026 provides an additional $5.5 billion to help the public health system meet front-line demand and deliver more services, including increased emergency department capacity, specialist assessment, elective surgery, cancer treatments, and GP visits, alongside targeted investments in paediatric palliative care, ambulance services, forensic mental health, and Pharmac.

It also commits $682 million in capital funding for health infrastructure, including a new 158-bed ward tower at Whangārei Hospital and the next stages of development at Tauranga, Hawke’s Bay and Palmerston North hospitals. Through this Budget, the Government is funding the purchase of land south of Auckland for a future new hospital, the redevelopment of the Mason Clinic in Auckland, and costs for the establishment of, of course, our new medical school at the University of Waikato. The starting age for free bowel screening will be lowered from 58 to 56 from the 30th of this month, and new mums will have the choice of longer postnatal stays thanks to this Budget.

We came into office promising to teach the basics brilliantly, and this year’s Budget continues efforts to boost educational achievement. Budget 2026 invests an additional $1.6 billion in operating funding for schooling and early childhood education, supports better opportunities for young people while helping to build a more productive, highly skilled workforce. Schools will receive increased operational funding, including support for higher employer KiwiSaver contributions, while early childhood education services will benefit from higher funding rates. The Budget also includes targeted investments to strengthen teaching and learning reading, writing, and maths, and to support the roll-out of a refreshed secondary curriculum and new national qualifications.

Next year, the Healthy School Lunches Programme will continue to offer students nutritious and affordable meals as ongoing work continues in the background for any potential future innovations in that programme. Budget 2026 also allocates $470 million of capital funding to redevelop up to 10 schools to deliver up to 232 additional classrooms and purchase land for new school sites in high-growth areas such as Queenstown.

This Budget ends the failed Fees-free scheme, which did not increase enrolments nor completion rates, especially for students from low-income backgrounds. The funding will now be put to better use to deliver front-line public services, including better prepared young people for trades and other vocational education. This Government will double trades academy places for year 11 to 13 students from 10,000 to 20,000 and provide 1,000 additional Youth Guarantee places offering wraparound support and training to school leavers with no or low qualifications.

This Government supports law and order, and through this Budget we’re providing a $1.1 billion uplift in the operating funding for Corrections, Customs, Police, and the Ministry of Justice to maintain essential front-line services that keep our communities safe. This includes funding of $477 million for Corrections to manage an increased number of prisoners, a $50 million funding boost for front-line policing, and investments to replace Police’s end-of-life automated biometric identification system. The Budget also provides funding to establish a new independent firearms regulator, Firearms Safety and Education New Zealand.
