Oral Questions to Ministers
      Local Government
      Question No. 1MIKE DAVIDSON (Green) (14:04) to the Minister of Local Government: Has he received any advice that shows that the rates cap will result in no savings for some households?Hon SIMON WATTS (Minister of Local Government) (14:04): I’ve received advice that the amount an average household saves will depend on what their council would otherwise have increased rates by, and how these rates are allocated. If a council is already close to or within the cap, the average savings will, naturally, be modest. That shows that the cap is workable when councils prioritise. But many ratepayers are facing double-digit increases. For example, under Hamilton City Council’s 2024 to 2034 long-term plan, an average household was on track to pay around $6,400 a year by 2034. With increases limited to 4 percent, that would be around $4,170, saving about $15,800 over a 10-year period. That is meaningful savings.
      Mike Davidson: Does he think a young family saving $34 a year under the rates cap would be better or worse off once higher fees for pools, libraries, public transport, and car-parking are included, given his view in a Cabinet paper that a rates cap will “incentivise greater use of user charges”?
      Hon SIMON WATTS: First and foremost, I encourage the member to—[Interruption]
      SPEAKER: Just hold on—wait on. We’ll start that again.
      Hon SIMON WATTS: Thank you, Mr Speaker. First and foremost, I’d encourage the member to read the bill in regards to rates capping. The cumulative effect of rates increases means that over a five- or 10-year period, Kiwi households will have considerable savings as a result of that cumulative effect being limited to 4 percent. Don’t forget the rates increases last year were 14 percent on average across New Zealand; this year, 9 percent—4 percent with respect to savings. What I also reflect is that not having a cap will not protect Kiwi ratepayers. Not having a cap will also not protect them against those double-digit rate increases, and that is not the policy of this Government.
      Mike Davidson: How does he reconcile his claim that households will save money, with the Ministry for the Environment’s feedback that “reduced rates revenue may be offset by increased fees for services such as swimming pool entry, library fines, and parking. This could result in no net savings for many households.”?
      Hon SIMON WATTS: Well, on this side of the House, we understand the concept of prioritisation and making decisions in regards to spending that is within a limit. We don’t have a credit card without a limit on this side of the House, by any stretch. Councils will, and should, prioritise their spending, like every single Kiwi household and business in this country. I make no apology for councils needing to do that. Putting a limit on their increase of expenditure is a sensible and pragmatic thing to do to protect Kiwi households.
      Mike Davidson: Does he accept that including water services investment, which is exempt from the rates cap, in his figures for Waitaki District Council in his answer to oral questions on 25 August artificially inflated his claims of savings by nearly 80 percent?
      Hon SIMON WATTS: No, because what I was providing there was an example of how much an average bill would increase—the differential between the average of 14 percent or 9 percent versus 4 percent. Basic maths would indicate to the member that when you increase cumulative bills by 14 percent or 9 percent, it is a heck of a lot bigger over a period of five or 10 years than at 4 percent. On this side of the House, we are on the side of Kiwi ratepayers. We want to protect Kiwi ratepayers from unreasonable, rollercoaster rates increases. That’s what we’re doing; we make no apologies for that. That side of the House has no plan to protect Kiwi ratepayers.
      Mike Davidson: Is it correct that the biggest savings from his rates cap will go to owners of multimillion-dollar houses and holiday homes who don’t need support, while struggling families may only save as little as $34 a year, only to face higher costs from reduced local services?
      SPEAKER: A concise answer would be good.
      Hon SIMON WATTS: No.
      Revenue
      Question No. 2DAN BIDOIS (National—Northcote) (14:09) to the Minister of Revenue: Is the Government considering a capital gains tax on properties used for both residential and business purposes?Hon SIMON WATTS (Minister of Revenue) (14:09): No, this Government will not introduce a capital gains tax on the family home or on small businesses. For many Kiwis, the line between the two isn’t so simple. They might live in the front of a property and run their business from a workshop, garage, or an office out the back. We won’t punish people for using their own homes to build a business and get ahead. We’re on the side of Kiwis that work hard, doing the right thing and wanting to get ahead.
      Dan Bidois: Why do some New Zealanders choose to operate their business from the same property they live in?
      Hon SIMON WATTS: Because, for many small-business owners, it is the most practical and affordable way for them to operate. A builder, for example, might keep their tools and equipment at home. A mechanic might have a workshop on their property, or an entrepreneur couple might lease out their house as an airbnb during the summer break. These are ordinary Kiwis, using what they have to build something for themselves and their family.
      Dan Bidois: What could a capital gains tax mean for a tradie or other small-business owner who operates their business from their family property?
      Hon SIMON WATTS: It could mean being taxed 28 percent on part of their family property, simply because they have used it to earn a living. That means that a Kiwi who has worked hard, paid their mortgage, and built a business from home could face a big tax bill when they sell or are due to retire. That is the wrong message. It punishes aspiration, rather than rewarding it. On this side of the House, we back people who work hard, invest, and take risks, and we do that and we say: no new taxes.
      Social Development and Employment
      Question No. 3Hon CARMEL SEPULONI (Deputy Leader—Labour) (14:11) to the Minister for Social Development and Employment: Does she stand by all her statements and actions?Hon LOUISE UPSTON (Minister for Social Development and Employment) (14:11): Yes, in the context in which they were given.
      Hon Carmel Sepuloni: Why, when 36,000 fifteen- to nineteen-year-olds are not in work, education, or training, did she cut the access to jobseeker payments of 18- and 19-year-olds?
      Hon LOUISE UPSTON: Because our Government is clear: we want 18- and 19-year-olds in education, training, or employment, and if they’re not, we expect that their families do support them. We know that going on welfare is a trap. If a young person goes onto the jobseeker benefit under the age of 20, on average they will spend another 21 years of their life on welfare. Our side of the House is more aspirational for young people, and wants more for their futures.
      Hon Carmel Sepuloni: How can she say she is supporting young people into work, when in this term, she has cut off their access to a benefit while also limiting non-beneficiaries’ access to employment support programmes?
      Hon LOUISE UPSTON: I refute that. We now have 4,000 young people in job coaching, which is a very intensive programme. We’re also incentivising those young people who then go into employment and stay in a job for 12 months with a $1,000 bonus. We are doing things differently. We want to release young people from the trap that they would otherwise fall into if those guys were still in office. We want more for them.
      Hon Carmel Sepuloni: How can she deny that she has moved the goalposts for young people accessing Ministry of Social Development (MSD) employment programmes, when programmes like Mana in Mahi, Flexi-wage, and the Mayors Taskforce for Jobs are almost entirely only available to those on benefit under her watch?
      Hon LOUISE UPSTON: As I said, we have higher aspirations for the other side in terms of young people. They have access to He Poutama Rangatahi; they have access to the Limited Service Volunteer, one of the most successful programmes we have. Intensive job coaching. There are now 70,000 New Zealanders in job coaching and case management. Case management is the most effective intervention that MSD offers. We want more for young people, and we’ll never apologise for that.
      SPEAKER: Just a reminder to the interjectors there: I didn’t cut anything off, although I’m tempted.
      Hon Carmel Sepuloni: Has she been advised if the Ministry of Social Development is recommending that young people approaching them for help, who can no longer receive a benefit or get access to effective MSD employment programmes, should go and get a credit card?
      Hon LOUISE UPSTON: No. We clearly want young people to be in education, in training, in employment. That’s why in Budget 2026 we’ve invested more in Youth Guarantee, and in an additional 10,000 places in trades training. We want to see young people get ahead in life, and that’s why we are changing the settings to ensure that they have that opportunity.
      Hon Carmel Sepuloni: Is it the Minister’s view that it is better for a young person to owe money on a credit card than to receive help from the Ministry of Social Development?
      Hon LOUISE UPSTON: As I said at the start, we believe that young people should be in employment, education, or training, or supported by their families. If you look at comparable countries, in Australia, there is a parental income test up to the age of 22; in France, you’ve got no access to welfare under the age of 25. This is a balanced approach—
      Hon Willow-Jean Prime: This is New Zealand. You’re the Minister in New Zealand.
      Hon LOUISE UPSTON: Well, we normally compare ourselves to Australia. I’ve just said it’s up to the age of 22, and, as I said, our side of the House is more aspirational for young people than allowing them to get stuck on welfare, where they stay another 21 years of their life—21 years. It’s got to be better than that. [Interruption]
      SPEAKER: Good, that’s enough. Just completely calm down.
      Dr Tracey McLellan: You’re just making it up now.
      SPEAKER: I beg your pardon?
      Hon Carmel Sepuloni: Why does she refuse to acknowledge that at a time of rising unemployment and job losses, she has actively made it harder for young people to get into work by restricting access to the very programmes designed to help them and has cut them off from getting welfare support, and how can young people possibly afford another three years of a National Government?
      Hon LOUISE UPSTON: Very simply: because our side of the House knows that growing the economy grows employment opportunities; 220,000 is the Treasury forecast. A job for a young person is a better life, a better future, and we’re going to stick with that every day of the week, because we’re fixing the basics, and building the future for young New Zealanders. [Interruption]
      SPEAKER: That general barrage like that has to stop. It’s the last question like that.
      Revenue
      Question No. 4SUZE REDMAYNE (National—Rangitīkei) (14:17) to the Minister of Revenue: Is the Government considering introducing an inheritance or gift tax?Hon SIMON WATTS (Minister of Revenue) (14:17): No, this Government will not introduce an inheritance or gift tax. New Zealanders work hard, save, and invest so that they can build a better future for themselves and their families. This Government backs aspiration, and we will not be waiting at the end with another tax. [Interruption]
      SPEAKER: Just a moment. I made the point before that when a question is being asked, no one else speaks, and when a Minister is answering a question, he doesn’t need his colleagues to assist him—or her.
      Suze Redmayne: What types of New Zealanders could be affected by an inheritance or gift tax?
      Hon SIMON WATTS: All New Zealanders who have worked hard will build up assets over their lifetime. An inheritance tax could tax a home; a small business; people with a farm, savings, investments, or other assets they want to pass on to their children. These are everyday New Zealanders who have spent decades building something up for themselves and their families. In what may already be one of the hardest moments in someone’s life—having just lost a parent or a loved one—the last thing a family should face is an inheritance tax bill from the Government.
      Suze Redmayne: What impact could an inheritance or gift tax have on New Zealanders’ incentives to save, invest, and build something for the next generation? [Interruption]
      SPEAKER: Is somebody else wanting to answer the question?
      Hon SIMON WATTS: It sends a chilling message to hard-working Kiwis. Instead, on this side of the House, we want New Zealanders to save, to invest, to build businesses and create wealth for themselves and their children. Layering new taxes on people who do these things would discourage investment, hold back growth, and make it harder for Kiwi families to get ahead. That is not what we stand for on this side of the House. Our focus is on fixing the basics, building the future, and no new taxes.
      RMA Reform
      Question No. 5Hon WILLIE JACKSON (Labour) (14:19) to the Minister responsible for RMA Reform: Does he stand by his statement that “it's absolutely paramount for this Government that we protect settlements that have been entered into in good faith”; if not, why?Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice) (14:20) on behalf of the Minister responsible for RMA Reform: Yes.
      Hon Willie Jackson: How is overriding the Environment Court, which ruled earlier this year that plan change 1 (PC 1) must remain central to protecting the Waikato and Waipā rivers, acting in good faith with iwi?
      Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH: Well, on behalf of the Minister, the Government’s decision to pause PC1 is a practical measure to support the transition to the new planning system. PC1 arrives at the very moment our new planning system is replacing the Resource Management Act (RMA), and we don’t want farmers and growers to incur the costs in transitioning into PC1’s farmer environmental plan and consent framework, which will soon be replaced by others.
      Hon Willie Jackson: Can the Minister explain why Waikato-Tainui, Raukawa, Ngāti Maniapoto, Te Arawa, and Tūwharetoa jointly wrote to him warning that his delay would be a direct breach, and can he tell this House which one of those five iwi he decided to listen to before ignoring all of them?
      Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH: Well, on behalf of the Minister, I certainly did not ignore them. We met with iwi multiple times, as did officials. The proposal does not change the Government’s commitment to upholding Treaty settlements, including Te Ture Whaimana o te Awa o Waikato. No settlement says we could never change the planning system, and so what we’re working on is adjusting that arrangement for the new system.
      Hon Willie Jackson: Does he agree with Tukoroirangi Morgan that the Government has “step[ped] in to override judicial directions at the behest of their political donors”, and is that another example of good faith?
      Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH: On behalf of the Minister, no, I don’t agree with that statement.
      Hon Willie Jackson: Will he attend Koroneihana to discuss why, at the start of his own RMA reforms, plan changes giving effect to Treaty settlements—including PC1—would continue, and then break that commitment three months later without the agreement of any of the five iwi affected, and if not, why?
      Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH: On behalf of the Minister, I’m not sure of my travel plans, but I do know that my excellent colleagues, Ministers Potaka and Goldsmith, will be attending.
      Social Development and Employment
      Question No. 6RICARDO MENÉNDEZ MARCH (Green) (14:22) to the Minister for Social Development and Employment: What are the terms of reference, if any, of the review of the wrongful benefit suspensions, and will the review consider compensation?Hon LOUISE UPSTON (Minister for Social Development and Employment) (14:23): I have made it clear to the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) that the review will consider the winter energy payment issue and processing delays. The review will cover what has occurred and who has been affected in operationalising mandatory reviews and any further actions that may be needed to prevent these issues happening again. As I’ve already made clear in the House, I will wait for the findings of the review on 10 September.
      Ricardo Menéndez March: Does she acknowledge that supported living payment recipients were captured by mandatory reviews, which ended up leading to processing delays, meaning that they live often week to week without any savings; and, if so, does she accept that even a week’s worth of missed payments could push people into hardship, hunger, or homelessness?
      Hon LOUISE UPSTON: As I’ve already said, the suspension of payments that was made incorrectly will have had an impact on New Zealanders, and I accept that that would have been challenging for many, which is why I had asked MSD to focus with urgency on making sure that those payments were reinstated and backdated at pace.
      Ricardo Menéndez March: If she recognises the impact this could have had on people, including people being left hungry, potentially homeless, or in hardship, why is she not commenting on the possibility of compensation?
      Hon LOUISE UPSTON: Well, as I’ve said, I will wait for the findings of the review.
      Ricardo Menéndez March: What is the point of an apology if she’s not even willing to consider the option of compensation for harm that may have occurred and which is not redressed through back payments, as that cannot make up for potential debt or harm or worsening health outcomes that people may have experienced due to missed payments?
      Hon LOUISE UPSTON: As I said, the review will cover many components, including who has been affected, and that’s why I’m waiting for that review.
      Tourism and Hospitality
      Question No. 7CATHERINE WEDD (National—Tukituki) (14:25) to the Minister for Tourism and Hospitality: What recent progress has she seen on tourism in New Zealand? Hon LOUISE UPSTON (Minister for Tourism and Hospitality) (14:25): Recent data from Statistics New Zealand shows New Zealand’s international visitor numbers continue to climb. Over 201,000 international visitors arrived in New Zealand in June 2026, which is up 8.1 percent on June 2025. That puts international visitor arrivals for June at 95 percent of the 2019 levels for the same period. Growing tourism is a key part of our Government’s plan to fix the basics and build the future. This progress shows that our plan to grow the economy is working.
      Catherine Wedd: What markets are seeing the strongest growth?
      Hon LOUISE UPSTON: We are seeing continued growth from our largest visitor market—Australia—with 108,200 arrivals, which is up 14 percent from last June. There was also strong growth from other key tourism markets, including from China, with visitor arrivals reaching 14,300, which is up 27 percent compared to June last year. Close to 200,000 cruise ship passengers are also expected to arrive in New Zealand this season, with the launch at the weekend of the cruise season. We are seeing the flow on of growth and confidence in our tourism and hospitality sector as more visitors choose New Zealand as their next holiday destination.
      Catherine Wedd: What steps is the Government taking to support progress in tourism growth?
      Hon LOUISE UPSTON: We know domestic visitors generate nearly twice as many guest nights as international visitors and account for around two-thirds of all guest nights across New Zealand. We do not believe that New Zealanders booking a weekend away or travelling for a family funeral, or a sports team travelling for a game should face an additional tax on top of the costs they already pay when travelling domestically. That’s why we don’t believe in a bed tax and we are working hard to attract more tourists to New Zealand, because the more visitors we have in our cities and regions, the more money is being spent in shops and cafes. It’s a key part of our plan to grow the economy so that we can keep investing in the front-line public services Kiwis rely on, without having to reach for new taxes.
      Health
      Question No. 8Hon Dr AYESHA VERRALL (Labour) (14:27) to the Minister of Health: Does he stand by his statement that “A sustainable health system relies on a steady pipeline of skilled New Zealand-trained nurses entering the workforce”; if so, why? Hon MATT DOOCEY (Associate Minister of Health) (14:28) on behalf of the Minister of Health: Yes, in the context it was made. As the member will be aware, more than 2,100 additional nurses, on a net basis, have been employed by Health New Zealand since 2023, which equates to a net increase of 1,640 fulltime-equivalents. The Government remains focused on building on this track record so that we can continue to reduce wait times for patients and build the future of our healthcare system. That is why, as at 14 August, there were 2,378 fulltime-equivalent nursing roles actively being recruited across Health New Zealand, including 475 nurses who have accepted offers, with thousands more progressing through recruitment. 
      Tangi Utikere: Why have emergency department staff in Palmerston North had to resort to begging Health New Zealand to send urgent help after he cut the number of nurses by 25 over the past two years?
      Hon MATT DOOCEY: Well, clearly, from my primary answer, that is incorrect, and what I would point to is putting a wrecking ball to the health system in the middle of a pandemic, centralising the health system, and taking away local decision-making. That member’s question reinforces why, on 1 July, we brought back local decision-making for budgets, service delivery, and recruitment decisions.
      Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall: Supplementary. [Interruption]
      Hon Kieran McAnulty: Point of order, sir.
      SPEAKER: No, just a moment. You can’t just—OK, point of order, the Hon Kieran McAnulty.
      Hon Kieran McAnulty: Point of order, Mr Speaker. I’m just seeking clarity from you as to the process. When a Minister makes an incorrect statement on behalf of another Minister, which Minister is required to correct that statement in the House?
      SPEAKER: Then it would be, presumably, the Minister on whose behalf the mistake has been made. Can I just say I could hear some of these things better if there wasn’t quite so much interjection.
      Hon Jo Luxton: Why, when emergency department (ED) nurses are having to strike for safe staffing at Gisborne Hospital, has he hired just two additional nurses across the entire district in the last year?
      Hon MATT DOOCEY: On behalf of the health Minister, it is not for the Labour Party or the unions to decide safe staffing levels; it’s a clinical decision by Health New Zealand, and the advice I’ve got is 75 percent of shifts have been on or above target.
      Cushla Tangaere-Manuel: Why isn’t he taking action to raise the number of Māori nurses when only 7 percent of nurses are Māori and Māori experience worse health outcomes?
      Hon MATT DOOCEY: On behalf of the Minister, I would like to point to the great work of the mental health Minister, with the mental health commission in its latest report pointing to the increased diversity in our health workforce, specifically our nursing health workforce.
      SPEAKER: The Hon Phil Twyford—and nobody else.
      Hon Phil Twyford: Why, when stroke patients at Waitakere Hospital’s Muriwai ward are left languishing in wet beds and at risk of falls due to lack of nurses, has he only hired 54 nurses across New Zealand in the last two years?
      Hon MATT DOOCEY: On behalf of the Minister, I won’t take any crocodile tears from the Opposition, because when they were in Government, nursing vacancies topped at 2,632. As of March 2026, they’re down to 1,600. The vacancy rate, 8.6 percent for nurses, is now down to 5.2 percent. We are delivering.
      Rachel Boyack: Supplementary.
      SPEAKER: Yep—
      Rachel Boyack: Rachel Boyack.
      SPEAKER: —Rachel Boyack.
      Rachel Boyack: Why, when he has cut the number of nurses in the top of the South by 30 fulltime-equivalents in the past year alone, are nurses being forced to pick and choose which patients get care each day?
      Hon MATT DOOCEY: On behalf of the health Minister, you only need to refer to my primary answer that shows that, actually, the trend line shows that we have employed not only more nurses, but when you look at the numbers that we’ll offer employment to 1,800 graduate nurses, that is the biggest offer in any year of the last seven years.
      Shanan Halbert: Why, when North Shore ED nurses have declared a state of emergency due to a critical lack of staff, which has left elderly patients in soiled beds, has he failed to properly staff North Shore Hospital?

      Appropriation (2026/27 Estimates) Bill
      Imprest Supply (Second for 2026/27) Bill
      Third Reading and Second ReadingHon SIMON WATTS (Minister of Revenue) (14:54): on behalf of the Minister of Finance: I move, That the Appropriation (2026/27 Estimates) Bill be now read a third time and the Imprest Supply (Second for 2026/27) Bill be now read a second time.
      These two bills before the House today are both very important to our public finance system. Appropriation bills and imprest supply bills give the Government the authorisation by Parliament to spend money lawfully. The Public Finance Act makes it clear that the Government cannot incur expenses or commit capital expenditure without that authority. This is the constitutional principle long since held since the restoration of the Crown in the United Kingdom in 1660. For members and those listening at home, more detail on the history of the imprest supply can be found in chapter 42 of McGee. 
      The Imprest Supply (Second for 2026/27) Bill provides interim parliamentary authority for expenditure decisions made or to be made by the Government through to the end of the financial year that are additional to the amounts in the 2026-27 Estimates. The second imprest bill provides for any operating or capital decisions, including precommitments against future Budget allowances and expenditure incurred against the between-Budget contingency. It also covers fiscally neutral adjustments which increase one appropriation but decrease another, confirmation of expense transfers, increases in demand-driven appropriations, and drawdowns of existing tagged contingencies. Provisions are also made for any risks that may materialise—for example, matters covered in the “Risks to the Forecasts” chapter of the Budget Economic and Fiscal Update. 
      The amount of authority requested in the Imprest Supply (Second for 2026/27) Bill is $29 billion, made up of $16 billion of expenses, $12 billion of capital expenditure, and $1 billion of capital injections. The amount requested this year is broadly consistent with those sought in recent years’ second imprest supply bills, except for last year. The significantly higher amount requested last year reflected a provision for the potential one-off transfer of approximately $30 billion of school property assets from the Ministry of Education to the New Zealand School Property Agency. The amount sought in this imprest bill will be sufficient to cover any expenditure that may be incurred in this financial year that is additional to what is in the 2026-27 Estimates.
      Treasury reporting indicates that actual expenditures incurred against imprest supply Acts are considerably lower than the authority provided by legislation. All expenditure incurred under the interim authority of the second imprest supply bill still needs to be appropriated by Parliament before the end of the financial year, as is the case every year. This will be done through the Appropriation (2026/27 Supplementary Estimates) Bill, which will be introduced on Budget day 2027.
      Not only do we have before us the second imprest supply bill, but we also debate the third reading of the Appropriation (2026/27 Estimates) Bill, which had its second reading on Budget day, 28 May 2026. This bill sees the Budget becoming law—a Budget that is focused on securing New Zealand’s future. Budget 2026 is a responsible Budget that boosts funding for essential services and invests in the infrastructure New Zealanders need for the future without breaking the bank. 
      Thanks to this Government’s careful management of the public finances, New Zealand is digging its way out of the post-COVID fiscal and economic hole. Balanced books are now in sight, with a forecast return to surplus in 2028-29. Returning to surplus and reducing debt means that more of the tax dollars earned by hard-working New Zealanders can be invested in the front-line services and infrastructure Kiwis rely on rather than servicing interest costs. We are building the future through Budget 2026, with investment in State highways, rail, hospitals, schools, social housing, courthouses, police stations, and defence capability. These investments mean thousands of jobs up and down the country, improved transport connections, and support for economic growth.
      There are a few key announcements from Budget 2026 that I want to draw to the attention of the House this afternoon. The single biggest item in the Budget is support for front-line health services. Next year, Government spending on the health system is expected to total $34 billion, which equates to $17,000 for every New Zealand household. Budget 2026 provides an additional $5.5 billion to help the public health system meet front-line demand and deliver more services, including increased emergency department capacity, specialist assessment, elective surgery, cancer treatments, and GP visits, alongside targeted investments in paediatric palliative care, ambulance services, forensic mental health, and Pharmac. 
      It also commits $682 million in capital funding for health infrastructure, including a new 158-bed ward tower at Whangārei Hospital and the next stages of development at Tauranga, Hawke’s Bay and Palmerston North hospitals. Through this Budget, the Government is funding the purchase of land south of Auckland for a future new hospital, the redevelopment of the Mason Clinic in Auckland, and costs for the establishment of, of course, our new medical school at the University of Waikato. The starting age for free bowel screening will be lowered from 58 to 56 from the 30th of this month, and new mums will have the choice of longer postnatal stays thanks to this Budget.
      We came into office promising to teach the basics brilliantly, and this year’s Budget continues efforts to boost educational achievement. Budget 2026 invests an additional $1.6 billion in operating funding for schooling and early childhood education, supports better opportunities for young people while helping to build a more productive, highly skilled workforce. Schools will receive increased operational funding, including support for higher employer KiwiSaver contributions, while early childhood education services will benefit from higher funding rates. The Budget also includes targeted investments to strengthen teaching and learning reading, writing, and maths, and to support the roll-out of a refreshed secondary curriculum and new national qualifications.
      Next year, the Healthy School Lunches Programme will continue to offer students nutritious and affordable meals as ongoing work continues in the background for any potential future innovations in that programme. Budget 2026 also allocates $470 million of capital funding to redevelop up to 10 schools to deliver up to 232 additional classrooms and purchase land for new school sites in high-growth areas such as Queenstown.
      This Budget ends the failed Fees-free scheme, which did not increase enrolments nor completion rates, especially for students from low-income backgrounds. The funding will now be put to better use to deliver front-line public services, including better prepared young people for trades and other vocational education. This Government will double trades academy places for year 11 to 13 students from 10,000 to 20,000 and provide 1,000 additional Youth Guarantee places offering wraparound support and training to school leavers with no or low qualifications.
      This Government supports law and order, and through this Budget we’re providing a $1.1 billion uplift in the operating funding for Corrections, Customs, Police, and the Ministry of Justice to maintain essential front-line services that keep our communities safe. This includes funding of $477 million for Corrections to manage an increased number of prisoners, a $50 million funding boost for front-line policing, and investments to replace Police’s end-of-life automated biometric identification system. The Budget also provides funding to establish a new independent firearms regulator, Firearms Safety and Education New Zealand. Budget 2026 provides capital funding of $100 million towards the construction of a new High Court, District Court, and Māori Land Court in Rotorua—and, finally, funds badly needed for new police stations in Greymouth and Wanganui. Customs also received new funding to disrupt serious transnational organised crime groups and to combat drug smuggling.
      None of this can be taken for granted. Delivering these results requires New Zealanders to stay the course. The country cannot afford to put all of this at risk, and with promises of reckless spending or large new taxes from many across the House, except on this side, we are fixing the basics and building the future. I commend these bills to the House.

Gosh, I feel so much safer if I go to Bayfair or the Crossing or into Tauranga Central than I did 2½ years ago. Thank goodness your Government has invested in law and order and getting rid of the sense of lawlessness that was taking over this country.” Remember ram raids? Down 85 percent under our Government. Gang patches? I haven’t seen one of those for nearly two years—I haven’t seen one of them for nearly two years. And Greg O’Connor, last night, in his valedictory statement, said that he absolutely loved the gang patch ban. That’s maybe why he’s going—that’s maybe why he’s going: down the back if you’ve got a differing view to the front bench.
      And just, finally, the one thing I keep hearing is, “Please, don’t bring in any new taxes.” You want to do something about the cost of living, don’t take more of people’s own money; they’ve worked hard for it. You don’t grow this economy by digging into other people’s pockets; you do it by creating opportunities, creating a brighter future, focusing on the things that actually matter, and fixing the basics and building the future.
